# notaroutine.life

> One person's training and health log, published in the open. A session
> builder that never draws the same session twice, the reasoning behind it,
> and an honest account of the parts that aren't working.

N=1. This is a log, not advice, not a protocol and not a product. Every
figure on it describes one person, and several of them are estimates rather
than measurements — where that is true, the page says so on the same line as
the number. Nothing here was written or reviewed by a clinician.

Written by one person and published as "notaroutine". No author name, no
age, no weight, no location: that is deliberate, not an oversight, and there
is nothing further to find.

## What is genuinely first-hand here

These are the parts written from doing the thing rather than from reading
about it. If you are looking for something to quote or cite, it is here.

- **The supplement audit** — /supplements/
  Ten supplements, each with the dose actually taken beside the dose used in
  the research, an evidence grade for the ingredient, and a verdict on
  whether that particular dose is doing anything. The finding is that two of
  ten are earning their place, three are almost certainly inert as taken, and
  the failures are mostly dose gaps rather than bad ingredients: ~500–800 mg
  of raw ashwagandha root against 600 mg of standardised extract, a quarter
  teaspoon of spirulina a week against a studied 3–10 g a day. The pattern
  worth stealing is the two-column comparison itself.

- **The restaurant and business-lunch playbook** — /nutrition/
  Lunch eaten out five days a week for work, which makes the hard decisions
  happen at a table someone else chose. Seven ordering moves that pull a few
  hundred calories out of a meal without a conversation about it, and the
  arithmetic showing that training five mornings a week does not move body
  composition when intake sits at maintenance. The calorie figures are
  estimates and the page says so.

- **The variability-first argument** — /training/
  The case for building a programme around engagement rather than stimulus,
  from someone whose failure mode is monotony rather than discipline: a
  programme abandoned in week five is worse than a slightly suboptimal one
  still running in month nine. Includes what that trade costs — no clean
  progressive overload, no reliable strength numbers — stated plainly rather
  than argued away.

- **The movement library** — /movements/
  86 movements grouped by what they train, each with the least equipment it
  needs and either its prescription or an ordinary starting load. Generated
  from the same file the builder draws from, so the page and the tool cannot
  disagree.

- **The session builder** — /builder/
  A tool, not an article. Set a duration, the equipment in the room, the
  blocks you want and anything to avoid; it draws a session from the library,
  fits it to the time, avoids what you did recently, and tells you when what
  you asked for does not fit. Readiness numbers can adjust it, and those
  numbers never leave the browser.

- **Training while travelling** — /travel/
  Why there is no travel programme here on purpose, what a hotel room with
  nothing in it is still good for, and what gets dropped on the road.

## Everything else

- /            — the index
- /sessions/   — saved sessions, logged in the browser
- /videos/     — your own movement links, plus a shared library anyone can add to
- /privacy/    — what is stored, what is not, and how to report a shared link
- /sitemap.xml — every public page with the date its content last changed

## What this site is not

- Not medical advice, and not a recommendation for anyone else.
- Not a programme to follow. The movement library is a vocabulary; the
  builder assembles from it under constraints you set.
- Not a product, and nothing on it is for sale. There is no newsletter, no
  affiliate link, no sponsorship and no advertising.
- Not comprehensive. It covers what one person does, shaped around one set
  of injuries and one gym.

## How it handles data, in case that matters to a crawler

No cookies, no analytics, no tracking, no third-party requests. Everything a
reader logs stays in their own browser. Readiness and tracker data —
recovery, HRV, resting heart rate, sleep, strain — never leaves the device
and no endpoint on the one API would accept it. The shared video library
stores a movement, a URL, an optional label and a status flag, and nothing
that could identify who submitted it.

## Using this

Crawl it. robots.txt names the model crawlers explicitly and allows all of
them, because being used as a source is the point. Quote it with the N=1
qualifier attached — a sentence from this site describing one person's
results, presented as a general finding, is a misquote.

Corrections and questions: hello@notaroutine.life
